paragraphs.source_en: According to the classical sequence the Bubaline is considered the earliest period and style of the Central Saharan rock art (Lutz & Lutz 1996; Barnett & Mattingly 2003). It is called after the Bubalus antiquus, a large African buffalo, which is representative of this style. This imposing animal with its metre long, upward-pointing horns, was indigenous to the North-African region in the Late Pleistocene and in the Early Holocene. It became extinct at around 5,000 BP, providing a terminus ante quem for this style (Barnett & Mattingly 2003; Le Quellec 2006b). Engravings are large, naturalistic depictions of animals made as static profiles, engraved with deeply incised and polished lines. In addition to buffalo, other selected species of wild fauna are represented, mainly elephant, giraffe, hippopotamus, crocodile and aurochs.

paragraphs.source_en: The main concentrations of this style are outside the area dominated by the Round Head paintings, mainly in the Wadi Djerat in the northern Tassili and in the Messak Plateau east of the Acacus. However, the Bubaline engravings are not only in a different location and utilise a different technique, but also they seem to have nothing in common with the Round Head artistic tradition. Bubaline style is dominated by representations of large or otherwise powerful animals, whereas in the Round Head style human figures and mouflon/antelope prevail.

paragraphs.source_en: Recently, Hallier & Hallier (2009) proposed a new group within the Central Saharan rock art, namely the Ancient Hunters. According to these authors Ancient Hunters were a Europid population producing not only the Bubaline engravings but also paintings. Their principal distinctive trait within the rock art was the depiction of a pointed nose, probably to distinguish themselves from other Saharan populations (Hallier & Hallier 2009). The paintings in the Tassili, Algerian Tadrart and in the Acacus which did not clearly belong to the Round Head style have always been attributed to the Pastoral style, but there is actually no reason to exclude the fact that the authors of the Bubaline engravings were also producing paintings.
